Formar o condicional simples (regulares: Form the simple conditional (regular and the ten irregulars) and use it to ask for things politely («¿Podría…?», «Me gustaría…», «Querría…»), to give advice («Deberías…», «Yo que tú…»), and to express wishes, without mixing up «pedir» and «preguntar».

PASSO 1: o condicional serve, entre outr: STEP 1: among other things, the conditional is used to ask, advise, and wish politely. The forms are easy to learn because they follow the future. STEP 2: take the whole infinitive (just like the future): «hablar», «comer», «vivir». STEP 3: add the conditional endings: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, -ían. They're the same for all three groups. «Hablaría, hablarías, hablaría, hablaríamos, hablaríais, hablarían.» All of them carry an accent on the «í». English has nothing like this ending system — its conditional is just "would" + the bare verb, the same for every single person, no suffix at all: "I would speak, you would speak, she would speak." Just like with the future, Spanish's six endings are new work, not a shortcut from anything in English. STEP 4: the ten irregular future verbs keep the same irregular stem in the conditional: «tendr-», «har-», «dir-», «podr-», «pondr-», «saldr-», «vendr-», «sabr-», «querr-», «habr-». Just change the ending: «tendría», «haría», «diría», «podría», «pondría», «saldría», «vendría», «sabría», «querría», «habría». STEP 5: every other verb is regular: «ser → sería», «ir → iría», «estar → estaría», «dar → daría», «ver → vería». STEP 6: the most common courtesy verb is «poder»: «¿Podría ayudarme?», «¿Podrías abrir la ventana?». STEP 7: the other two are «gustar» and «querer»: «Me gustaría un café», «Querría hablar con usted». «Gustaría» takes an indirect object pronoun, just like «gusta» (lesson 16): «Me gustaría», «Te gustaría», «Le gustaría». STEP 8: «quisiera» (lesson 8) is another courtesy form. It belongs to a tense called the subjunctive, which we'll get to later; for now, just use it as a set phrase: «Quisiera un café». «Querría» and «quisiera» are equivalent here. STEP 9: object pronouns go before the conjugated verb, or attached to the infinitive: «¿Me podría ayudar?» and «¿Podría ayudarme?» are both correct.
em português, o condicional também se fo: Spanish's conditional ending really is a suffix tacked onto the full infinitive (or the same irregular stem the future uses), which means building a whole new ending set, the way the future did — English's single invariant "would" offers no shortcut here. What does echo something familiar is the courtesy use itself: English "would" softens requests the same way («Could you help me?», «I would like a coffee»), so the function is instantly recognizable even if the grammar underneath isn't.
I would like a coffee with milk.
I would like to speak with the director.

PASSO 1: para aconselhar com suavidade,: STEP 1: to give advice gently, use the conditional of «deber» and «poder»: «Deberías dormir más», «Podrías hablar con tu jefa». The conditional softens the advice; «Debes dormir más» sounds like an order. STEP 2: the formula «Yo que tú» + conditional is very common: «Yo que tú, hablaría con ella», meaning "if I were you, I'd talk to her." There's also «En tu lugar» + conditional: «En tu lugar, no iría». STEP 3: with «usted», the formula changes: «Yo que usted, esperaría» or «En su lugar, esperaría». STEP 4: «sería mejor» + infinitive, or «sería mejor que» + subjunctive (coming later): «Sería mejor salir pronto». STEP 5: to express a wish, use «Me gustaría», «Me encantaría» (I'd love to), «Querría»: «Me encantaría conocer Sevilla.» STEP 6: the conditional also marks politeness when asking for information: «¿Sabría decirme dónde está la estación?» (Would you happen to know where the station is?). STEP 7: don't use the conditional to give an order. For a request among friends, the present is just as natural: «¿Me pasas la sal?» Use the conditional when you want to be more careful, or with people you don't know. STEP 8: don't mix up these two verbs: «pedir» means to request or order something («Te pido un favor», «Pido un café»), and «preguntar» means to ask a question («Te pregunto una cosa»). Someone requesting something doesn't use «por»: the object comes straight after, «pedir un café».
em português diz-se «Você deveria dormir: English runs on the exact same two formulas: "You should rest more" softens the same way «Deberías» does compared to the blunter "You must rest," and "If I were you, I'd talk to her" matches «Yo que tú, hablaría con ella» almost word for word. This whole lesson's logic transfers cleanly — the harder part is just remembering that «pedir» and «preguntar» split what English's single verb "to ask" covers, so you have to pick the right one every time English wouldn't force you to.

PASSO 1: a mesma coisa pode ser pedida d: STEP 1: the same thing can be asked for in several ways, from the most direct to the most polite. With a friend: «Dame la llave» (direct), «¿Me das la llave?» (natural), «¿Me puedes dar la llave?». STEP 2: with someone you don't know, or in a formal setting: «¿Podría darme la llave?» or «Quisiera la llave, por favor». STEP 3: to ask for something difficult or inconvenient, use «¿Le importaría…?» (for «usted») or «¿Te importaría…?» (for «tú»): «¿Le importaría hablar más bajo?». STEP 4: «¿Sería posible…?» also works, with the infinitive: «¿Sería posible cambiar de habitación?» STEP 5: to explain a problem politely, don't point fingers: «Hay mucho ruido en la habitación» is gentler than «Usted hace mucho ruido». STEP 6: to thank someone and wrap up: «Muchas gracias por su ayuda», «Se lo agradezco mucho». STEP 7: false friend: «oficina» means office; an auto repair shop is «taller». STEP 8: «cuarto» and «habitación» both mean room; «cuarto de baño» is the bathroom. In a hotel, «habitación» is more common; at home, «cuarto» or «habitación».
